e.t: This word means “field”: an area of land outside a town or dwelling, often understood as open or cultivated ground. It is a noun naming a physical place rather than an action or quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 227 times, so it commonly identifies land in ordinary descriptions, ownership, travel, and work. Its precise significance in any verse comes from surrounding context.

This adjective means “non-discriminatory.” It describes a person, action, or judgment that does not make discriminatory distinctions. As an adjective, it identifies a quality belonging to something rather than naming an object or expressing an action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Proverbs 32:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

Azour or Azur is a proper name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it marks a specific named reference rather than expressing a general concept. The name occurs twice in the LXX, both in Nehemiah: Nehemiah 3:19 and 10:18. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not establish the particular person or setting in either verse; that requires the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “unmoved” or “motionless”: remaining still rather than changing position. It can describe something fixed in place or otherwise not moving. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, in Exodus, Job, and 3 Maccabees, so its central sense is consistent but its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse. The word functions as a description of a person or thing characterized by stillness, not as an action or command.

This adjective describes something absurd or unreasoning—something that lacks sound sense or does not arise from reasonable thought. It can characterize a person, action, or idea, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Wisdom, 3 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what it modifies and the surrounding wording.

Amorri is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament, referring to a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its meaning is presented simply as “Amorri,” so it should be understood as a name, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word. This LXX word occurs once, in Judges 10:8. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain exactly whom or what the name identifies in that passage.

Aniel is a personal name, also represented as Anil. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs two times, in Numbers 34:23 and 1 Chronicles 7:39. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in each passage cannot be described further, but its basic function remains that of a person’s name.

This verb means to withhold wrongfully—keeping back something that another person is rightly owed. It describes an unjust refusal to give what is due, rather than a neutral act of delaying or retaining something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 24:14, and functions as an action word describing wrongful withholding. Its precise force in that passage is understood from the surrounding verse and its concern for just treatment.

ἀποδοχεῖον means “storehouse” or “granary”—a place where goods are kept. It is a noun naming a storage building rather than the goods themselves. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in Sirach. Its central idea is a physical repository for supplies. In each passage, the surrounding verse determines the particular detail, but the basic meaning remains the same.

This verb means “bathe off.” It describes an act of washing by bathing, expressing removal through that action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 9:30. The word’s basic sense is focused and concrete: it points to bathing as an action of washing off. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “deprive”: to take away something from a person or leave someone without what is due. It describes an action of withholding or removing, rather than simply lacking something. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Malachi, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being taken away and from whom. “Deprive” is the clearest supported English meaning.

This verb means “pour out,” describing liquid being released from one container or place into another, or emptied freely. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in three separate verses, showing a specific but repeated vocabulary for the act of pouring. Its precise force in a particular passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding words.

This Greek LXX noun means “silver plate,” referring to a flat or plated object made of silver. It names a physical item rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 15:32. That single occurrence confirms its ordinary lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the object’s specific role in that passage. Its meaning is therefore straightforward: a silver plate or silver-plated item.

Arphaxad is a proper name—the name of a person in the biblical genealogies. The name appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, all in genealogical records: six occurrences are in Genesis and one is in 1 Chronicles. It identifies the same named ancestor across those records rather than describing a quality, action, or object. The alternate rendering “Arfaksath” refers to the same name. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding genealogy.

This word means "chief of the eunuchs," a noun naming the leading official among eunuchs. It appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament, all in Daniel 1. The word functions as a title or office designation rather than a personal name. Its precise responsibilities in any particular verse depend on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning identifies a chief official within the group of eunuchs.

Assouriim, also rendered Assurim, is a proper name identifying a person or people rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 25:3. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to the named figure or group in that passage. The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely whom the name identifies there.

This word means “just as” or “so as,” linking an action or description to something else in a sentence. It functions as an adverb, helping express comparison or the manner in which something occurs. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it appears once, in 3 Maccabees 1:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is to connect ideas by comparison or manner.

This Greek LXX word means “deep.” As an adjective, it describes something reaching far downward or inward; as an adverb, it can describe depth or intensity. Its use can therefore refer to physical depth or to something difficult to reach or fully search out, depending on the sentence. It occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. The surrounding verse determines whether the word describes depth in a literal or figurative way.

Barakim, also rendered Varakim, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Samuel 3:16. Because it functions as a personal or place name in the text, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes the person or location being mentioned. The name itself does not provide enough information to establish a broader spiritual or descriptive meaning.

Basou, also rendered Vasu, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:17. The available information identifies the name clearly but does not provide the verse text or enough surrounding context to explain who this person was or what role he held. Its meaning is therefore best understood as a personal designation, with the exact historical reference depending on the passage in Ezra.

This word is a proper name rendered “Bēthsour” or “Vithsur.” It identifies a named person, place, or other proper designation rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:16. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided, its precise referent in that passage cannot be explained further from the word alone. The spelling reflects a name preserved through Greek rendering, not an ordinary vocabulary term.

This LXX Greek verb means “fare” or “have a lifestyle”—to live or conduct one’s life in a particular way. It describes a person’s manner of living rather than merely the fact of being alive. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, appearing in Job, Proverbs, Wisdom, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun refers to the stomach or the womb, and can describe a woman who is pregnant. Its basic sense concerns the body’s inner place where food is held or where a child develops. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 64 times, so its meaning is established across many passages rather than being limited to one unusual use. The surrounding sentence determines whether it refers to the physical stomach or to pregnancy. This word appears in passages from Genesis, Exodus, Judges, and other books.

This adjective means “geometrical,” referring to something connected with geometry, measured shapes, lines, or spatial arrangement. It describes rather than names a person or thing, so its precise force depends on the noun or idea it modifies. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Zechariah 2:5. The word’s basic sense is therefore precise and technical: it points to geometry or geometric measurement rather than expressing an emotion, action, or moral quality.

Gersam, also rendered Yirsam, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies the same named individual wherever it occurs, rather than describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears six times in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus and 1 Chronicles. Its occurrences include genealogical and family records, but the name itself does not express a general idea or activity. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s specific role in each passage.

This Greek LXX adjective means “right,” describing the right-hand side, direction, or position. It is used across the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense appears in many kinds of statements rather than referring to one special subject. The word occurs 210 times in this LXX corpus, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what person, object, or direction the surrounding sentence identifies.

This noun means “deliberation”—the process of carefully considering a matter before a decision or course of action. It refers to purposeful thought rather than a passing idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across Psalms, Ezekiel, and Hosea. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains deliberate consideration or planning.

This verb means to “give a hearing”—to listen to someone or allow a matter to be heard. It describes an act of attentive consideration rather than merely possessing the ability to hear. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy 1:16 and Job 9:33. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains granting attention or a hearing to a person or matter.

This Greek LXX verb means “pour through,” describing something being poured or flowing through an opening, channel, or material. It presents an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with especially frequent use in Leviticus. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being poured and what it passes through, but the central idea remains movement through something by pouring.

This is a proper name, appearing as “Dōsitheos” or “Thositheos,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Esther 10:3. The name is preserved in transliterated form, but no further ordinary lexical definition is provided. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone.

This Greek Old Testament adjective describes something that is “possessed” or “acquired.” It points to what has been obtained or is held as someone’s property, functioning as a describing word rather than naming an action. In the Septuagint, it occurs three times, twice in Leviticus and once in Numbers. The precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is possession or acquisition.

This adjective means “heavy with child” or “pregnant.” It describes a woman who is carrying a child, focusing on her bodily condition during pregnancy. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Sirach 42:10. Its basic meaning is clear even though the available English rendering there is brief; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the word functions in that particular sentence.

This verb means “throw into; put into,” describing an action that moves something or someone into a place or situation. It focuses on the act of placing or casting inward, rather than merely being present there. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense remains an inward movement caused by deliberate action.

This verb means “pierce”: to push or drive something through a person or object. It describes an action that breaks through or penetrates rather than merely touching or striking. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs eight times, always expressing this direct action. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what is being pierced and the surrounding sentence.

Emath is a proper name for a place mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object; rather, it identifies a particular location in the biblical record. The name appears seven times, across seven Old Testament verses, including passages in Numbers, Joshua, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Amos, and Zechariah. Because Emath is a place-name, the surrounding passage is needed to understand the significance of that location in any particular verse.

This verb means “indicate” or “demonstrate”: it describes making something clear or showing it plainly. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, it can describe a person or action that points something out so it may be recognized. It occurs 12 times, across Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Daniel, and other books. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being shown and the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “activate” or “active”: it describes something becoming effective, functioning, or exerting activity. As a verb, it can express the action of making something work or the state of being active. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages from Numbers, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any verse depends on what person or thing is described as active or being activated. [p03:word:lxx:L704718:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L704718:occurrences]

ἐνταῦθα is an adverb meaning “in that place; here.” It points to a location, directing attention to where someone or something is, happens, or should be found. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to the place being discussed or to the speaker’s present location. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 28 times, showing its ordinary use as a straightforward word for location rather than an action or quality.

This verb means to deny utterly—to completely reject or disown something rather than merely question it. It expresses a strong refusal in which the person gives no acknowledgment or acceptance. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:35. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a decisive and complete denial.

This noun means “close examination” or “scrutiny”—a careful, searching inspection of something. It describes more than a quick look, pointing to attention given in order to examine matters thoroughly. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but the central idea remains careful investigation rather than casual observation.

“Dig out/through” describes the action of excavating, removing material, or making a passage by digging. It is a verb used for a physical action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs twice, in 1 Samuel and Proverbs. The central idea remains purposeful digging through or out of something; the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording. Its meaning is therefore concrete and active: something is being opened, cleared, or penetrated by digging.

This verb means “bloom” or “be in flower.” It describes a plant coming into bloom or displaying its flowers. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 14:7, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not available here. The word presents flowering as a visible stage of renewed or active plant life, rather than as a person’s action or a general feeling. Its precise force in Job depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “scream out”—to call or cry aloud with force. It describes vocal expression that is loud and urgent rather than quiet speech. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and speaker, but its central idea remains an emphatic cry made openly and audibly.

This verb means “fill up again”: to make something full once more or bring it back to fullness. It describes a repeated act of filling rather than a first filling. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one sentence depends on what is being filled and the surrounding context, but the central idea remains renewed fullness.

This noun means “inspection” or “visitation,” referring to an act of examining or visiting. Its precise emphasis depends on the surrounding sentence: it may identify the act itself rather than a person or place. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs 60 times, with most occurrences in the Old Testament portion and additional occurrences in deuterocanonical books. The word appears especially often in Numbers, where its repeated use reflects the language of counting or examining people. It is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

This Greek LXX verb means “taskmaster,” describing the act or role of driving people to perform assigned labor. It presents someone as an overseer who presses workers to complete their tasks, rather than simply describing ordinary work itself. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in 2 Chronicles 8:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a person who directs and compels labor.

This word refers to the evening, or to something occurring at evening. It functions as a noun naming that time of day rather than describing a person, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job, showing a focused use for the evening period. Its basic meaning remains simple: it identifies the time when day moves toward night. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wording.

This word is a proper name identifying “Euergetes,” also given as “Everyetis.” It functions as a personal name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs six times across five verses, including Esther, Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. The supplied material establishes the name and its use, but not an expanded meaning beyond this identification.

This adjective means “spacious,” describing something that has ample room or breadth. It can refer to a place or area understood as broad rather than confined. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, including passages in 2 Chronicles, Psalms, Isaiah, and Hosea. Its central idea remains the same wherever it appears: roominess, openness, or considerable extent. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is described as spacious.

This noun means “amber,” the name of a substance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Ezekiel, so its use is limited rather than a broad term appearing throughout that corpus. The lexical meaning remains the same wherever it occurs: it identifies amber itself. The surrounding verse determines what is being described with it, but the word’s basic sense is simply “amber.”

Theko is a proper name, referring to a particular person or place identified by that name. It is not presented as a word describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, Theko occurs once, in Joshua 15:59. Because no verse text or wider context is available here, the name’s specific referent cannot be determined from this lexical entry alone. Its meaning is therefore best retained as the name “Theko.”

This Greek LXX noun means “brought-up,” referring to someone who has been raised or brought up. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Esther 2:7. Its basic sense points to a person’s upbringing or the condition of having been brought up, rather than naming an action performed in the moment. The precise force of the word in that occurrence depends on the surrounding context of Esther 2:7.

This noun means a “healer”: a person whose role is to treat sickness and bring healing. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Leviticus and Job, so it names a recognized kind of person rather than an action or quality. The word’s basic meaning stays focused on someone who provides healing; the surrounding verse determines how that role is being discussed.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iedia” or “Iethia.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or common object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:37. The available information establishes the name and its occurrence, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or enough surrounding verse text to explain anything more about the person named.

Iemouēl; Iemoil is a proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears four times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in genealogical passages associated with Genesis, Exodus, and 1 Chronicles. Its significance in any particular verse depends on the person being named there, but the word itself functions as a personal designation. It is not presented here with an additional lexical definition beyond the name forms “Iemouēl; Iemoil.”

Iesboam, also rendered Iezvoam, is a proper name for a person. It functions as a name rather than as a word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles: 12:7 and 27:2. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself identifies the person but does not provide further information about his role or significance. The two approved forms, “Iesboam” and “Iezvoam,” represent the same recorded name.

gl: render equal rights; render what is due
d: render equal rights; render what is due

e.t: This verb means to render equal rights or to give each person what is due. It describes an action of granting fair treatment or an appropriate share, rather than merely recognizing that people are equal. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:24. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central idea is administering what is rightfully owed or deserved.

This LXX adverb means “categorically,” expressing something stated in an absolute, definite way rather than tentatively or partially. It describes how a statement or assertion is made, marking it as firm and unqualified. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Ezekiel, Daniel, and Amos. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a categorical or absolute assertion.

This Greek LXX verb means “constrain”: to limit someone’s freedom of action or compel a person to do something. It describes an exerting of pressure rather than a simple request or invitation. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Genesis 19:3 and once in Exodus 12:33. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its central idea remains the same: another person is pressed or compelled rather than acting entirely freely.

This Greek verb means to “shut up” or “confine”—to keep someone or something enclosed so that movement is restricted. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, it appears five times, including uses in Jeremiah, Wisdom, and Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding passage says is being enclosed.

This Greek LXX verb means “slander”: speaking about someone in a harmful or dishonoring way. It describes speech that attacks another person’s reputation rather than simply reporting facts. The word is used 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from Numbers through Malachi. As a verb, it expresses the act of slandering or speaking against someone. Its exact force in any individual verse is clarified by the surrounding passage.

This verb describes acting “very earnest”—with intense seriousness and wholehearted effort. It presents earnestness as something a person does, rather than merely a feeling or opinion. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Job 23:15, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: to approach something with exceptional seriousness, urgency, or devotion rather than casually or halfheartedly.

This verb means to shower something down upon a person or place like hail. It expresses a forceful falling or pouring from above, using hail as the picture for the action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 2:15, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains a heavy, descending shower rather than a gentle sprinkling.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “twist by spinning” or “spin.” It describes the action of turning fibers together to make thread or cord. The word is used 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, most often in Exodus, where descriptions of sacred furnishings and priestly clothing involve spun material. As a verb, it focuses on the making or preparation of thread through spinning, rather than naming the finished cloth or cord. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This adjective describes something secret or hidden—kept out of sight, concealed from people, or not openly known. It can describe a matter whose full meaning or purpose is not immediately disclosed. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 20 times, showing a recurring word for what is concealed rather than openly displayed. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “ring” or “circle,” referring to a rounded form or a circular path. It is a noun used for something shaped in a loop or understood as moving around a circuit. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across eight verses, including descriptions connected with lands, repeated movement, architectural features, and the shape of a city or region. Its precise sense in any particular verse is determined by what the surrounding passage describes.

gl: thigh bone with the flesh on it; ham
d: thigh bone with the flesh on it; ham

e.t: κωλέα refers to the thigh bone together with the flesh on it—the ham. It is a noun naming a specific portion of an animal’s leg, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 9:24. The word’s precise significance in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical sense is clear: a meaty thigh portion prepared as food.

The word refers to tree-moss or lichen, a growth found on trees and other surfaces. It is a noun naming this particular natural substance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus, at Leviticus 21:20 and 22:22. The word’s basic meaning remains the same in both references; the surrounding verse determines how that named condition relates to the passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “prayer” or “entreaty”—an earnest appeal directed to someone for help, favor, or action. It names the appeal itself rather than the person making it. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX material represented here, across 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea remains a serious request or plea, with the surrounding passage determining what is being requested and to whom the appeal is directed.

This LXX Greek particle means “in affirmation.” It functions as a brief confirming expression, marking agreement or strengthening an assertion rather than naming an object, action, or person. Its meaning is therefore concise and supportive: it affirms what is being said. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 10:15; the surrounding verse text is not available here, so its precise force in that sentence depends on the context.

Madebēna is a proper name rendered as “Madebēna” or “Mathevina.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Isaiah 10:31. Without the verse text or wider passage, Scripture here does not provide enough information to explain more about the person or place designated by the name. Its meaning is therefore chiefly its identifying function: it names Madebēna, also represented as Mathevina.

This word is an adjective that describes a quality or condition. Its basic sense is “long time”. It describes something extended over a considerable span rather than brief or momentary. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in passages connected with the promise of an enduring outcome. Its use in Exodus and Deuteronomy shows that it helps describe duration in a straightforward way. The word itself does not specify every detail about that duration; the surrounding sentence supplies the particular application.

This Greek LXX verb means “stand aside; remove.” It describes moving out of the way or taking something or someone away. The word appears 27 times in the Greek LXX, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its central idea is an action of separation or displacement rather than a fixed object or person. The surrounding sentence determines whether the action is understood as standing aside or removing something.

This adjective means “greater,” describing something that exceeds another in size, importance, strength, age, status, or degree. It is a comparative word, so it normally presents one person or thing as surpassing another rather than simply describing greatness in isolation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, mainly in the Old Testament portion of the corpus. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being compared.

This noun means “change of purpose; regret”—a turning from an earlier intention accompanied by sorrow or reconsideration. It names an inward change rather than an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Hosea 11:8. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context, but its central idea remains a changed purpose or regret. It should therefore be understood as describing a shift in intention, not merely a passing feeling.

This noun means “new month,” referring to the beginning of a fresh monthly cycle. It names a point in the calendar rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 24 times, with nearly all occurrences in Old Testament books and one in a deuterocanonical book. Its use is connected with dates, appointed observances, and recurring monthly occasions, while the surrounding passage determines the specific significance in each verse.

Ozazias is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears as a proper name in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once in the LXX, at 2 Chronicles 31:13. The name itself is not presented here with an expanded definition or description, so its ordinary function is simply to identify the person who bears it. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s role there.

This word refers to the site or grounds where a house stands. As a noun or adjective, it describes a house’s location rather than the building’s interior or its occupants. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Psalms and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any one passage depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the idea of a house site.

This noun refers to an “observer” or “beholder”—someone who watches or sees. It describes a person in the role of looking on, without by itself stating what is being observed or why. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs twice, both times in Job. Its ordinary sense remains focused on the one who observes. The surrounding passage determines the particular force of the word in either occurrence, but the basic meaning is a person who beholds or observes.

This Greek LXX noun describes a forceful inner movement—an “impulse” or “indignation.” It can refer either to a strong surge that presses toward action or to intense displeasure stirred by a situation. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its central idea is a powerful emotional or motivating force rather than a mild feeling. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun refers to an “absolute monarch”—a ruler whose authority is not limited by another earthly governing power. It identifies a person by the supreme character of his rule, rather than describing an action or feeling. In the Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs once, in Sirach 50:15. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is a ruler possessing absolute authority.
